thread.title: Sony To Dance To Only Slightly Different Tune Under New CEO - Sony Corporation (NYSE:SNE)

author: Nick Cox
title: Sony To Dance To Only Slightly Different Tune Under New CEO - Sony Corporation (NYSE:SNE)
text:
Sony Corp ( SNE ) is placing increased emphasis on music under new CEO Kenichiro Yoshida. Recent moves by him illustrate Sony's determination to remain the world's largest music publisher. At the same time he has made it clear that Sony will continue to emphasize its market-leading position in image sensors and in gaming consoles.
In March last year my article saw Sony putting its emphasis on these areas. So it has turned out to be as the stock price has climbed ever upwards. Sony should be seen as still being a growth company with low valuations. It remains a strong Buy.
The Sound of Music. Rather as expected, Sony announced in late-May they had bought the interests held in EMI by Mubadala Investments of Abu Dhabi for US$3.66 billion. Some considered this a high price at 19 times EBITDA but it gives the company 90% of EMI.
New CEO Yoshida said the purchase was:
"A particularly significant milestone for our long-term growth".
UBS recently forecast the streaming revenues for music publishers would rise to US$3.6 billion by 2026. This would be up from US$700 million last year. Sony is in prime position to benefit from this. It was thus willing to pay the price to Mubadala to ensure this pole position. Sony also has a highly profitable stake in Spotify ( SPOT ).
The importance of Music to Sony is shown by its 2017 results as below:
Sony web-site
Sony's Music division turnover has increased 109% in the past three years. It is a vital cog in what makes Sony a growth company.
For some years now companies have been trying to work out how to accrue income from music under the new Internet paradigm. The growth and value of music streaming now puts Sony at the forefront of how to make money out of music. This is reminiscent of the old days when the Sony Walkman dominated the music agenda. Sony has the added advantage of a very strong and growing animation business which is folded into its Music offering.
As my article in October last year pointed out, Sony is looking to be the "Digital Entertainment Hub" for the all-important youth dynamic. This enables them to bring together music, PS4 & gaming, and movies. This makes for a seamless offering that is dominating its field. The image sensor division ensures Sony maintains its technical lead over its rivals and continuously opens up new growth areas.
Every Picture Tells a Story Yoshida has also been making some changes to the Pictures division. He recently announced a slew of executives who were being let go, and other cost-cutting measures. This is unlikely to presage a sale of the division. Many analysts have predicted this for some years and will almost certainly be proven wrong again. There is a lot of merger talk around at the moment over the big studios, so nothing is certain in the industry. However Yoshida has recently stated he sees Pictures as being one of the company's major growth areas.
Only last month the company acquired a stake in Peanuts Holdings, who have the rights to the cartoon characters Snoopy and Charlie Brown. Leveraging film rights from franchises to media opportunities such as gaming and TV is one way the company is headed. This has been successfully done, for instance, with the "Jumanji" franchise.
It seems the company does not want to get involved in a costly direct content war with the likes of Netflix (NFLX ) or wannabe content provider Apple ( AAPL ).
The Picture division remains an integral part of their digital entertainment hub. In the last 18 months the division has started to perform somewhat better as my article in August pointed out. However the emphasis in future is likely to be on its complementary role with the other business divisions. One particular area of fast-growing strength is in the Media Network division, especially in India. This was recently emphasized by the company. The synergies for Sony are almost endless.
PS4 remains the market-dominating games console. The PSVR is the best-selling virtual reality headset, though the general sales of VR headsets in the market has disappointed . Sony will continue to develop this line with a new VR headset expected next year. If virtual reality takes off as its proponents hope, Sony should remain at the forefront.
At the same time they will focus their efforts on cloud gaming. This will ultimately take over from console gaming and physical games. Sony needs to maintain its market leadership position there. As was emphasized in the company's "Corporate Strategy for 2018-20" released in May, PlayStation Network is a focal point of concentration for the next few years.
The other jewel in the crown for Sony is its image sensor division. Sony dominates the mobile phone market for these. Image sensors are also at the core of future product development for the company. This includes for robots, for autonomous vehicles, for AI and for medical imaging equipment. This provides almost endless possibilities for the company. A recent example is their announcement for a taxi-hailing service in Japan using the company's A1 technology.
In May Yoshida announced about 1 trillion yen (US$9 billion) to be invested in this division. Sony's strong and profitable position in image sensors is unlikely to be challenged anytime soon. It is a costly and technically difficult area for a new competitor to penetrate.
Valuations Sony has continued to be under-rated by analysts.
As per figures from Charles Schwab (subscription required), its low valuation is starkly highlighted if you compare Sony with S & P Global BMI Consumer Discretionary index:
PE = 13.75 (S & P 17.79).
Forward PE = 12.78 (S & P 17.15)
Price to Sales = 0.77 (S & P 1.16)
Price to Cash Flow = 7.25 (S & P 12.03)
The company has even reverted to paying a dividend. It is at only 0.71% but the company intends to continue to increase its dividend yield after years of cutting out unprofitable divisions.
Apart from dividend increases, Yoshida has stated some mid-term ambitions. These include producing 2 trillion yen (US$18 billion) of operating cash flow within 3 years from the non-financial divisions of the company. They also include generating an annual return on equity of over 10%. He expected Music, Pictures and Semiconductors to continue strong profit growth. He predicted PS profit growth to slow as hardware became more competitive and as the company moves more towards services and intellectual property.
The 2 trillion yen of operating cash flow can be contrasted with expected capital investment of 1 trillion yen. For shareholders this leaves the enticing prospect of 1 trillion yen to strengthen the balance sheet and increase dividends.
These recent projections last month by Yoshida were criticized by some analysts as being too conservative. Many of them marked down Sony's Buy ratings. They mirror what happened after the annual results were published at the end of March. Then the stock price fell on similarly conservative comments, but rose again after people looked at the details. The same thing happened again after the latest comments by Yoshida. The analysts have a long history of getting Sony's stock price projections very wrong. Investors would have done well to buy Sony stock each time it falls on bearish comments from analysts.
Conclusion As with any companies there are risks to the stock price. My recent article detailed some of these.
My investment target is always to find companies with strong Management in secular growth areas which are worthy of long-term investment. Sony continues to tick these boxes for me. Visionary CEO Kazuo Hirai revolutionized the company as a previous article of mine detailed . He is still there as chairman.
New CEO Yoshida is in the enviable position of being able to build on this very solid platform. The growth potential of the company's key divisions is great. Sony is dominating in all three of game consoles, music and image sensors. That makes further stock price gains very likely, despite the strong rises already seen over the past couple of years,
Disclosure: I am/we are long SNE.
